REFLECT · BAND LOG

APOLLO MOON MUSIFICATION

Tranquillitatis · Procellarum. An endless seismic band and a living map of the near side of the Moon: ISM-02 of Interplanetary Seismic Musification, the pair of ELYSIUM MARS. Six days recorded by the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment at two stations become a band in A at 99.375 BPM: S11 at Tranquility Base in Mare Tranquillitatis (Apollo 11, July–August 1969) and S12 in Oceanus Procellarum (Apollo 12, 1969–1977). The pictures come from real lunar topography.

THE STATIONS

S11 was a solar-powered seismometer that Buzz Aldrin set up near the Lunar Module Eagle. It recorded for about three weeks and slept through the lunar night. S12, nuclear-powered, recorded for almost eight years, until NASA switched the network off on 30 September 1977. The two stations are about 1,400 km apart and never listened at the same time: S11 fell silent in August 1969, three months before S12 began. Every meeting between them in this piece is composed.

THE TERRAIN DATA

The elevations come from the MoonTopo2600p spherical-harmonic model of the Moon's shape (M. A. Wieczorek, 2015), the lunar sibling of the MarsTopo719 model behind ELYSIUM MARS, here as the 10′ grid published by Fatiando a Terra (CC BY 4.0). A regional tile at 1/6° (about 5 km) covers 15°N–15°S, 40°W–40°E, from Oceanus Procellarum to Mare Tranquillitatis, with Copernicus (93 km wide) near its centre. A 0.5° global grid draws the globe. In this model the Copernicus rim stands about 0.3 km above the reference surface and its floor about 3.2 km below it; the real crater is about 3.8 km deep, so the 10′ grid smooths it a little. S11 sits at about −1.7 km and S12 at about −1.2 km. Blue marks low ground below −0.9 km: the maria (the dark basalt "seas") and the deepest crater floors.

THE BAND

Each station has its own line-up. S11: Room 1969.207 (lunar noon, near silence), Singer 1969.214 (late-day pops before the night shutdown), Rhythm 1969.202 (impulsive events the day after landing). S12: Room 1975.066 (flat mode, Earth-commanded pulse trains), Singer 1969.324 (the ascent stage of LM Intrepid striking the surface 76 km away at 22:17:17.7 UTC), Rhythm 1973.072 (a large shallow moonquake). Each file is cut to a 75-minute window and loops in its own time, so the three drift against each other forever. Each singer's strongest minute becomes its station's naive melody.

The Apollo sampling clock is the tempo: one 16th note is one MHZ sample (1/6.625 s), one beat is one four-sample telemetry frame (0.604 s), so 99.375 BPM. Chords change every 3 bars; the melody cell is 11 eighths long (Apollo 11); the bass and hand-drum ostinato is 12 eighths long (Apollo 12). All the loops realign every 132 bars = 11 × 12, at HOME, on A. At the 960× standard the seismometer's own 2.2-second pendulum resonance sounds at 436 Hz, close to A4, so the instrument sets the key. Each HOME cycle is one hour of a lunar day (29.53 Earth days long): thermal moonquakes crackle sharply at sunrise and broadly at sunset, as they did on the Apollo records, and the night belongs to earthshine. Every 90 bars (90 frames make one Apollo telemetry block) a new set begins at the other station: Rainbow, Curved Air, Poppy Nogood, Surveyor, Broken, Drone and Launch. The singer's echo is 2 beats long, 1.21 s: inside the 1.2–1.4 s it takes light to cross from the Moon to Earth.

LAUNCH SEQUENCE

Press 月 and the piece counts down for 16 bars (T−16 … T−1) before the band enters. A sequencer pulse starts dark and sparse, string pads swell, an octave-pulse bass enters halfway, an ignition swell rises through the last bar, and at liftoff the band begins set 1 while the camera climbs from Copernicus into orbit. Neither Apollo 11 nor Apollo 12 heard its own launch: the S11 liftoff (17:54 UTC, 21 July 1969) falls in a telemetry gap, and the S12 liftoff (about 14:25 UTC, 20 November 1969) sits in a disturbed, gapped stretch. The Launch set brings the same voices back in the rotation. These are the first ISM voices made with oscillators, not seismic grains: sawtooth and pulse waves through resonant low-pass filters, in the style of 1980s analog-sequencer space synth. No source recording is quoted. The sequencer walks each station's own melody cell, the room's energy opens the filter, and the rhythm's zero crossings place the accents. Every 16th step is one Apollo sample.

PHASE

A layer after SEIST3RRY, an earlier SE1STR0N1CA instrument. Three to five voices play one shared cell of 6–8 notes, each a hair faster than the last (up to about 3%, more when the rhythm event is busy), so they slide out of step the way Riley's In C players do. At every HOME they snap back onto the grid on A. The cell keeps to two or three degrees of the scale, a harmonic territory, and moves to the next one when the data surge or the dwell runs out, always on a chord change. It avoids its last three notes and leaps for contrast. Each voice is a grain of a different band member's own moonquake, so the phasing sounds like the Moon, not like a synth. Under it, dervish sines sit on just ratios over A (1 · 3/2 · 2 · 3 · 4), detuned by how long each quake rings so they beat slowly, and their panning rotates. The layer grows in the lunar night and when the band falls quiet. On screen, small glyph rings orbit the station, one per voice, and drift apart; a white ring flashes when they meet at HOME.

Repeatable: one seed, APOLLO MOON MUSIFICATION · ISM-02, drives every choice, and decisions follow the musical clock, not the screen. A fresh Begin plays the same piece.

AFTER TERRY RILEY

The musical model is Terry Riley's A Rainbow in Curved Air, released in 1969, the year of Apollo 11 and Apollo 12: modal organ lines in odd-length cells over a steady pulse, a hand drum and a tambourine, layers piling up through Riley's time-lag accumulator (two tape machines feeding each other). The Poppy Nogood set is named after the record's B-side. No Riley melody is quoted. As in ELYSIUM MARS, the seismic data never choose free pitch or timing; they choose touch: velocity, density, which safe note, when the melody grows or shrinks, how bright each voice is.

WHAT YOU SEE

Sun: the lunar clock lights the relief. There is no air, so the sky stays black and the terminator is hard; at night only earthshine remains. Melody: every note lights a contour ring inside Copernicus at its own depth, so the melody climbs the crater wall. Dum shakes the ground, the tambourine sparks around the active station, the Curved Air runs are micrometeorite flashes, and pulses travel between the two stations. At HOME an ensō is drawn around the Copernicus rim. Every scene opens in lunar night, and the summits catch the sunrise first. Scenes: Rise (a low orbit of Copernicus, with Earth in the sky), Plains, Crater, Orbit. Modes: Hybrid, ASCII paint-by-numbers (as in ELYSIUM MARS) and Pixel. Black, white and blue only.

DATA AND HONESTY

The waveforms are the 2022 re-archive of the Apollo data (Nunn, Nakamura, Kedar and Panning), bundled as untouched MiniSEED records and decoded in your browser by the ELYSIUM parser. The archive fills gaps with −1; they are interpolated, and residual spikes are repaired. Event descriptions come from inspecting the waveforms. Local lunar time is computed from the Moon's mean elongation and is good to about half an hour. You can drop any other Apollo XA day-file into Controls; its strongest 75 minutes will join the band.
